lesson.title: Six Hundred Sextillion: Making Sense of Avogadro's Number
lesson.summary: Avogadro's number, 6.022 x 10^23, is the fixed count of particles in one mole, the bridge that lets chemists convert between the number of atoms or molecules and a mass they can actually put on a balance.
lesson.body:
Atoms and molecules are so small that even a speck of dust contains more of them than there are stars in the observable universe. If a chemist tried to count out atoms one at a time, even at a rate of a million per second, it would take far longer than the age of the universe to weigh out a useful sample. Chemistry needed a counting unit the way everyday life needed the idea of a dozen, except this unit had to be enormous, because the objects being counted are unimaginably tiny and light. That unit is the mole, and the number that defines it is Avogadro's number.

Avogadro's number is 6.022 x 10^23, usually written with four significant figures as 6.022 x 10^23 and known to more precision as 6.02214076 x 10^23 particles per mole. One mole of any substance, whether it is atoms of iron, molecules of water, or ions of chloride, contains exactly this many individual particles. The number is named after Amedeo Avogadro, an Italian scientist who proposed in 1811 that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Avogadro never measured the number itself; that came almost a century later through the work of several scientists, including Jean Perrin, who used measurements of Brownian motion and other physical methods to pin down its value and named it in Avogadro's honor.

The size of this number is not arbitrary. It is defined so that the mass of one mole of a substance in grams equals the average atomic or molecular mass of that substance expressed in atomic mass units. This is the essential link between the mole concept, which defines a mole as a counted quantity of particles, and molar mass, which lets that quantity be measured on a balance instead of counted directly. Because of this connection, Avogadro's number is the conversion factor that moves a chemist between the particle view of matter, individual atoms and molecules, and the macroscopic view, grams that can be weighed in a lab.

Consider a sample of 3.50 mol of iron atoms. To find the number of individual atoms, multiply by Avogadro's number: 3.50 mol x 6.022 x 10^23 atoms/mol = 2.11 x 10^24 atoms of iron. The same relationship works in reverse. Suppose a sample contains 1.20 x 10^24 molecules of carbon dioxide. Dividing by Avogadro's number gives the amount in moles: 1.20 x 10^24 molecules / 6.022 x 10^23 molecules/mol = 1.99 mol of carbon dioxide. Notice that the unit mole cancels correctly in both directions, which is a useful check that the calculation is set up properly.

Every later mole-based calculation in chemistry, from finding the mass of a reactant to predicting the volume of a gas produced in a reaction, ultimately rests on this single fixed number. It converts the abstract, countable idea of a mole into something concrete: a specific, enormous quantity of atoms, molecules, or ions that never changes no matter what substance is being discussed. Learning to move fluently between moles and number of particles using Avogadro's number is the first skill that makes every later mole calculation possible.
